IN-CLASS · Q1

Licence plates

A plate begins with S, followed by two uppercase letters, four digits and one uppercase letter. How many plates are possible?
Show answer
Product rule over eight positions: 1 · 26 · 26 · 10⁴ · 26 = 26³ · 10⁴ = 175,760,000.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule (AND): a valid outcome is built position by position; multiply the number of choices at each position.

Step 1. Draw one slot per position and write how many symbols may go in it: S | 26 | 26 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 26. The first slot has exactly 1 choice (it must be S).

Step 2. Every slot is filled independently of the others (choosing the first letter does not change the choices for the digits), so the rule is AND: multiply. 1 × 26 × 26 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 26.

Step 3. Group the equal factors: 26 × 26 × 26 = 26³ = 17,576 and 10⁴ = 10,000. 17,576 × 10,000 = 175,760,000.

Check / common slip. Do not add the slot counts (that would be the sum rule). Letters are 26 choices, digits are 10; the fixed “S” contributes ×1.

IN-CLASS · Q2

Non-taxi plates

Plates beginning with SH are reserved for taxis. How many plates remain for non-taxis?
Show answer
Subtract the reserved set: 26³·10⁴ − 26²·10⁴ = 169,000,000. With S and H fixed, one letter, four digits and a final letter vary.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.5 Complement: when the direct case is awkward, count everything then subtract the cases you do not want. Here “all plates” − “taxi plates”.

Step 1. All plates were counted in exercise 1: 26³ × 10⁴ = 175,760,000.

Step 2. Taxi plates start S, H. Now two slots are fixed (×1 each) and the remaining slots are one letter, four digits, one letter: 26 × 10⁴ × 26 = 26² × 10⁴ = 6,760,000.

Step 3. Non-taxi = 175,760,000 − 6,760,000 = 169,000,000.

Check / common slip. Direct check: the second letter may be anything except H, so 25 choices instead of 26: 25 × 26 × 10⁴ × 26 = 169,000,000. Same answer, which confirms the complement method.

IN-CLASS · Q3

Passwords with at least one digit

How many case-insensitive alphanumeric passwords of length 6, 7 or 8 contain at least one digit?
Show answer
Complement rule for each length k: 36ᵏ − 26ᵏ (all strings minus letters only). The lengths are mutually exclusive, so add: (36⁶−26⁶)+(36⁷−26⁷)+(36⁸−26⁸) = 2,684,483,063,360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.5 Complement (“at least one” = all − none) combined with §1.3 Sum rule (the three lengths cannot overlap).

Step 1. “At least one digit” is awkward to count directly (one digit? two? …). Count its opposite instead: passwords with no digit, i.e. letters only.

Step 2. For one length k: all alphanumeric strings = 36k (26 letters + 10 digits, case-insensitive); letters-only strings = 26k. So “at least one digit” = 36k − 26k.

Step 3. A password has exactly one length, so lengths 6, 7, 8 are separate cases: add (sum rule). k=6: 2,176,782,336 − 308,915,776 = 1,867,866,560. k=7: 78,364,164,096 − 8,031,810,176 = 70,332,353,920. k=8: 2,821,109,907,456 − 208,827,064,576 = 2,612,282,842,880.

Step 4. Total = 2,684,483,063,360.

Check / common slip. Subtract inside each length, then add. Do not subtract at the very end of a combined total.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Starts with a or ends with z

Using lowercase letters and digits, how many 6-character passwords start with a or end with z?
Show answer
Inclusion–exclusion: |A| = 36⁵, |Z| = 36⁵, |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴, so 36⁵ + 36⁵ − 36⁴ = 119,252,736.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.4 Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, because a password in both sets is counted twice when you add.

Step 1. Set A = “starts with a”: first slot fixed, five free slots of 36 choices: 36⁵ = 60,466,176. Set Z = “ends with z”: also 36⁵.

Step 2. Passwords in both A and Z have the first and last slot fixed, four free slots: |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴ = 1,679,616.

Step 3. “Or” here means at least one of them, so |A ∪ Z| = 60,466,176 + 60,466,176 − 1,679,616 = 119,252,736.

Check / common slip. Adding only |A| + |Z| double counts every password that starts with a and ends with z; that is why you subtract the overlap once.

IN-CLASS · Q5

Keeping A, B and C together

How many permutations of A to H keep ABC consecutive? What if A, B and C stay together in any internal order?
Show answer
Treat the three letters as one block, giving six objects. Exactly ABC: 6! = 720. Any internal order: 6! · 3! = 4,320.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.8 Block method: glue the objects that must stay together into one super-object, arrange the objects, then arrange inside the block if allowed.

Step 1. Glue A, B, C into one block “ABC”. Now you have the block plus D, E, F, G, H: 1 + 5 = 6 objects.

Step 2. Arrange 6 objects in a row: 6! = 720. The block is fixed as exactly ABC, so there is no inside arrangement: 720.

Step 3. If A, B, C may be in any internal order, multiply by the 3! = 6 ways to arrange the letters inside the block: 720 × 6 = 4,320.

Check / common slip. The most common slip is counting 8! and trying to subtract. The block method counts the good arrangements directly.

IN-CLASS · Q6

Four diners, six seats

Four diners occupy four of six distinct seats. How many seating arrangements are there?
Show answer
Order matters: P(6,4) = 6!/2! = 360. Equivalently choose then arrange: C(6,4) · 4! = 15 · 24 = 360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations: choose and order r of n distinct items, P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!. Seats are distinct, so order matters.

Step 1. Seat diner 1: 6 seats. Diner 2: 5 left. Diner 3: 4 left. Diner 4: 3 left. By the product rule: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360.

Step 2. That product is exactly P(6, 4) = 6!/(6−4)! = 720/2 = 360.

Step 3. Second route (§1.7 then §1.6): first choose which 4 of the 6 seats are used, C(6, 4) = 15, then arrange the four diners in them, 4! = 24: 15 × 24 = 360. Both views must agree.

IN-CLASS · Q7

Forming the committee

How many 7-member committees contain 3 faculty chosen from 40 and 4 students chosen from 300?
Show answer
Two independent selections, so the product rule gives C(40,3) · C(300,4) = 3,268,216,809,000.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule over two independent choices, with §1.7 Combinations because a committee has no order.

Step 1. Pick the faculty members: a group of 3 from 40, order irrelevant: C(40, 3) = 9,880.

Step 2. Pick the students: 4 from 300, order irrelevant: C(300, 4) = 300·299·298·297 / 4! = 330,791,175.

Step 3. The two choices are independent (AND), so multiply: C(40, 3) × C(300, 4) = 3,268,216,809,000.

Check / common slip. Do not use P(n, r): swapping two faculty members gives the same committee, so order must not be counted.

IN-CLASS · Q8

No two women adjacent

How many ways can 3 men and 3 women stand in a line if no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Arrange the men (3!), which creates 4 gaps. Choose 3 of the 4 gaps and arrange the women: 3! · C(4,3) · 3! = 6 · 4 · 6 = 144, which equals 3! · P(4,3).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.9 Gap method: place the unrestricted objects first; the restricted objects can only go into the gaps between them.

Step 1. Line up the 3 men first: 3! = 6 ways. They leave 4 gaps: _ M _ M _ M _.

Step 2. No two women adjacent means each woman gets her own gap. Choose which 3 of the 4 gaps are used: C(4, 3) = 4.

Step 3. Arrange the 3 distinct women in those gaps: 3! = 6. Multiply: 6 × 4 × 6 = 144.

Step 4. Same thing written as 3! × P(4, 3) = 6 × 24, because choosing and arranging 3 of 4 gaps is P(4, 3).

Check / common slip. If you put the women in first you create gaps for the men and the answer changes meaning. Always place the unrestricted group first.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q1

Multiple-choice test (Rosen 6.1 Q3)

A test has 10 questions with 4 possible answers each. In how many ways can a student answer if every question is answered? If blanks are allowed?
Show answer
Every question answered: 4¹⁰. Blanks allowed: each question has 5 options, so 5¹⁰.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule: each question is an independent slot.

Step 1. 10 questions, each answered in 4 ways: 4 × 4 × … × 4 (ten times) = 410 = 1,048,576.

Step 2. If a question may also be left blank, each slot has 4 + 1 = 5 options (sum rule inside one slot): 510 = 9,765,625.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q2

Integers 100 to 999 (Rosen 6.1 Q23)

How many integers from 100 to 999 inclusive: divisible by 7; odd; with three equal digits; not divisible by 4; divisible by 3 or 4; divisible by neither 3 nor 4; divisible by 3 but not 4; divisible by 3 and 4?
Show answer
In order: 128; 450; 9; 675; 450; 450; 225; 75. For example, 3 or 4: 300 + 225 − 75 = 450, and 3 and 4 means divisible by 12, which gives 75.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2–1.5: count by division and complement over the range 100–999, which has 900 integers.

Step 1. Multiples of m in a range: ⌊999/m⌋ − ⌊99/m⌋. Divisible by 7: 142 − 14 = 128.

Step 2. Odd: every second integer is odd, 900 ÷ 2 = 450. Three equal digits: 111, 222, …, 999 = 9.

Step 3. Not divisible by 4: multiples of 4 are 249 − 24 = 225, so 900 − 225 = 675 (complement).

Step 4. §1.4: multiples of 3 = 333 − 33 = 300; multiples of 4 = 225; multiples of both means multiples of 12 = 83 − 8 = 75. 3 or 4 = 300 + 225 − 75 = 450.

Step 5. Neither 3 nor 4 = 900 − 450 = 450. 3 but not 4 = 300 − 75 = 225. 3 and 4 = 75.

Check / common slip. Words to translate: “or” = union (add then subtract the overlap), “and” = intersection (here, divisible by the lcm 12), “neither” = complement of the union.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q3

Two licence plate formats (Rosen 6.1 Q29)

How many plates can be made from either 2 letters then 4 digits, or 2 digits then 4 letters?
Show answer
Sum rule over two disjoint formats: 26²·10⁴ + 10²·26⁴ = 52,457,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.3 Sum rule (OR): when an outcome fits exactly one of two disjoint formats, add the counts of each format.

Step 1. Format 1 (2 letters then 4 digits): 26 × 26 × 10⁴ = 6,760,000.

Step 2. Format 2 (2 digits then 4 letters): 10 × 10 × 26⁴ = 100 × 456,976 = 45,697,600.

Step 3. A plate cannot be both formats, so no overlap to subtract: 6,760,000 + 45,697,600 = 52,457,600.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q4

Circular seating, neighbours only (Rosen 6.1 Q45)

Seat six people around a circular table where two seatings are the same if everyone has the same two neighbours, ignoring left and right.
Show answer
5!/2 = 60: fix one person to remove rotations, then halve to ignore reflections.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.10 Circular arrangements: rotations of the same seating count as one, so fix one person and arrange the rest.

Step 1. In a row there would be 6! = 720 arrangements. In a circle each seating appears 6 times (once per rotation), so divide by 6, or equivalently fix one person and arrange the other 5: 5! = 120.

Step 2. The question also says a seating and its mirror image are the same (same two neighbours for everyone). Each seating is counted twice, so divide by 2: 120 ÷ 2 = 60.

Check / common slip. Ask each time: do rotations count as different? do reflections count as different? The answer changes the divisor.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q5

Wedding photograph (Rosen 6.1 Q47)

Six people stand in a row, including the bride and groom. How many ways if the bride must be next to the groom; not next to the groom; to the left of the groom?
Show answer
Next to each other: block method 5! · 2 = 240. Not next to: 720 − 240 = 480. Bride somewhere left of the groom: half of all orders, 720/2 = 360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.8 Block method for “must be next to”, §1.5 Complement for “not next to”, symmetry for “left of”.

Step 1. Next to each other: glue bride and groom into a block (2 internal orders). 5 objects: 5! = 120, times 2 for the block’s inside order = 240.

Step 2. Not next to each other: all arrangements 6! = 720 minus the “next to” ones 240 = 480.

Step 3. Bride left of groom: in exactly half of all arrangements the bride is left, in the other half the groom is: 720 ÷ 2 = 360. (No counting of positions needed, just symmetry.)

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q6

Permutations ending in a (Rosen 6.3 Q3)

How many permutations of {a, b, c, d, e, f, g} end with a?
Show answer
Fix the last letter and arrange the other six: 6! = 720.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations with a fixed position: a fixed position removes one choice slot.

Step 1. The last position must be a: 1 choice. The other six letters b…g fill the six remaining positions in any order: 6! = 720.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q7

Alternating men and women (Rosen 6.3 Q13)

A group has n men and n women. In how many ways can they stand in a row if men and women alternate?
Show answer
Choose which sex starts (2 ways), then arrange each sex: 2 · (n!)².
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule with a first choice and §1.6 arrangement inside each group.

Step 1. Alternating means the pattern is MWMW… or WMWM…: 2 choices for which sex starts. (Both patterns exist only because the counts are equal.)

Step 2. Once the pattern is fixed, arrange the n men in the n men-slots: n!. Arrange the n women in the n women-slots: n!.

Step 3. Total = 2 × n! × n! = 2 · (n!)².

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q8

Ten coin flips (Rosen 6.3 Q19)

A coin is flipped 10 times. How many outcomes are there in total, with exactly two heads, with at most three tails, and with equal heads and tails?
Show answer
Total 2¹⁰ = 1,024. Exactly two heads C(10,2) = 45. At most three tails C(10,0)+C(10,1)+C(10,2)+C(10,3) = 176. Equal heads and tails C(10,5) = 252.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule (2 per flip), §1.7 Combinations (choose which flips are heads), §1.3 Sum rule over cases.

Step 1. Total outcomes: each of 10 flips has 2 outcomes: 210 = 1,024.

Step 2. Exactly two heads: choose which 2 of the 10 flips are heads: C(10, 2) = 45. The rest must be tails, so there is nothing else to choose.

Step 3. At most three tails: the cases 0, 1, 2 or 3 tails are disjoint, so add: C(10,0) + C(10,1) + C(10,2) + C(10,3) = 1 + 10 + 45 + 120 = 176.

Step 4. Equal heads and tails: 5 heads and 5 tails, C(10, 5) = 252.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q9

8 men and 5 women, no two women adjacent (Rosen 6.3 Q23)

How many ways can 8 men and 5 women stand in a line so that no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Place the men first (8!), which creates 9 gaps. Place the women in gaps: P(9,5). Total 8! · P(9,5) = 609,638,400.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.9 Gap method (same method as exercise 8 with bigger numbers).

Step 1. Line up the 8 men: 8! = 40,320. They create 9 gaps (one before, one after, seven between).

Step 2. Each of the 5 women goes in a different gap, and order matters (the women are distinct): P(9, 5) = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 = 15,120.

Step 3. Multiply: 40,320 × 15,120 = 609,638,400.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q10

Club of 25 members (Rosen 6.3 Q27)

How many ways are there to choose 4 members for an executive committee, and to choose a president, vice president, secretary and treasurer with no person holding two offices?
Show answer
Committee: order does not matter, C(25,4) = 12,650. Offices: order matters, P(25,4) = 303,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 vs §1.7: ask “does the order of the chosen people matter?”. A committee has no roles; officers do.

Step 1. Four-member executive committee: the four are interchangeable, so combinations: C(25, 4) = 25·24·23·22 / 4! = 12,650.

Step 2. President, VP, secretary, treasurer: roles are different, so swapping two people gives a different outcome: P(25, 4) = 25 × 24 × 23 × 22 = 303,600.

Step 3. Notice 303,600 = 12,650 × 4!: every committee can be given its four jobs in 4! = 24 ways.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q11

Cinema seating

19 students occupy a row of 22 seats. How many ways? If Andrew, Brandon and Cheryl join (22 students in 22 seats) and Brandon sits at either end, how many ways?
Show answer
First part P(22,19) = 22!/3! ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰. Second part: 2 end seats for Brandon, then the other 21 people fill 21 seats, 2 · 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations for part 1; §1.8 fix-the-end idea (a position restricted to 2 seats) for part 2.

Step 1. 19 students into 22 distinct seats, order matters: 22 × 21 × … × 4 = 22!/3! = P(22, 19) ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰.

Step 2. Now 22 students and 22 seats. Brandon must take one of the 2 end seats: 2 choices.

Step 3. The other 21 students fill the other 21 seats in any order: 21!. Total = 2 × 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q12

10 men and 10 women

How many ways are there to arrange them in a row? How many ways to seat all 20 at two circular tables (one blue, one red) with 5 men and 5 women alternating at each?
Show answer
Row: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸. Two alternating tables: (C(10,5)·C(10,5)·4!·5!/2) · (C(5,5)·C(5,5)·4!·5!/2) ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹. The answer key says rounded values are for reference; the formula is what you must produce.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 (row), then §1.7 + §1.10 (circular, alternating) built from smaller counted pieces.

Step 1. Row: 20 distinct people in 20 positions: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸.

Step 2. Two tables, each with 5 men and 5 women alternating. First decide who sits at the blue table: choose 5 of the 10 men, C(10, 5), and 5 of the 10 women, C(10, 5). The rest go to red (C(5,5) = 1 each).

Step 3. At one table: seat the 5 men around the circle (circular, so fix one: 4!), then the 5 women go into the 5 gaps between them: 5!. The answer key also divides by 2, treating a seating and its mirror image as the same, as in the earlier circular question. So per table 4!·5!/2 = 1,440.

Step 4. Multiply all: C(10,5)² × 1,440 × 1,440 = 63,504 × 1,440 × 1,440 ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹.

Check / common slip. The key states rounded numbers are for reference. In the exam, show the formula and the factors; each factor comes from one counting rule.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
IN-CLASS · Q1

Complexity of an exam-style recursion

What is the time complexity of z(n) when each call loops n times calling z(n-1)?
Show answer
T(n) = n · T(n−1), which unrolls to n!, so O(n!).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.6 Recurrences (unroll the recurrence) and §2.4 Complexity classes (factorial).

Step 1. Each call z(n) runs a loop of n iterations and each iteration calls z(n−1): so T(n) = n × T(n−1).

Step 2. Unroll: T(n) = n × (n−1) × T(n−2) = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × T(n−3) = … = n × (n−1) × … × 1 = n!.

Step 3. n! is its own complexity class, far above exponential: O(n!).

Check / common slip. A loop that calls the function inside it multiplies the cost of the call by the number of iterations. A loop followed by a call would add.

📚 Tutorial questions

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q1

Counting steps from a table

A table gives, for each input value, the number of times an operation is performed (the count is the input plus a constant). What is the Big O?
Show answer
O(n): the number of operations grows linearly with the input, and the constant offset is dropped.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.3 Growth rate: read the pattern of how the count changes when the input grows by 1.

Step 1. The table shows count = input + constant (for example 5, 6, 7, … for inputs 0, 1, 2, …). Each step of 1 in the input adds 1 to the count.

Step 2. A constant increase per unit input is linear growth. The constant offset does not change the shape (§2.5 drop constants), so O(n).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q2

Simplify the step counts

Give the Big O of: (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N, (b) N² + 2N − 3, (c) N! + 100N²⁰, (d) 2ᴺ + N!, (e) 5N log₂N + N√N, (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)², (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N².
Show answer
(a) O(N²); (b) O(N²); (c) O(N!); (d) O(N!); (e) O(N^1.5) because N√N beats N log N; (f) O(N² log N); (h) O((log N)²). Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constants.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.5 Dominance rules: keep only the fastest-growing term; drop constant multipliers and slower terms.

Step 1. Use the growth order from slowest to fastest: 1 < log N < (log N)² < √N < N < N log N < N^1.5 < N² < N² log N < N³ < 2N < N!.

Step 2. (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N: the fastest term is N², so O(N²). (b) N² + 2N − 3: O(N²).

Step 3. (c) N! + 100N²⁰: factorial beats any polynomial no matter how large the exponent: O(N!). (d) 2N + N!: N! wins: O(N!).

Step 4. (e) 5N log₂N + N√N: N√N = N^1.5 grows faster than N log N (a power of N beats a log), so O(N^1.5).

Step 5. (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)²: N² log N dominates: O(N² log N). (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N²: constants and the log terms are slower than (log N)², and log N² = 2 log N is just a log: O((log N)²).

Check / common slip. Constants like 100 or 0.02 never change the class. The question is always “what happens when N is huge?”.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q3

Three loop shapes

Give the complexity of: two loops in a row over n and m; a nested n × n loop followed by a single n loop; and a loop where the inner while j > i runs from n down to i.
Show answer
Two loops in a row: O(n + m) or O(max(n, m)). Nested then single: O(n²). Dependent inner loop: n + (n−1) + … + 1, so O(n²).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns: sequential blocks add, nested blocks multiply, a dependent inner loop is a sum 1 + 2 + … + n.

Step 1. Two loops one after another, over n then over m: n + m steps, written O(n + m) (or O(max(n, m))).

Step 2. A nested n × n loop (n² steps) followed by one loop of n steps: n² + n, and the dominant term is n²: O(n²).

Step 3. Inner loop depends on i (runs n − i times): total = n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, and dropping the 1/2 and lower term gives O(n²).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q4

f, g and h

f(n) sums 1..n−1 in a loop. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and calls f(i) each time. h(n) returns f(n) + g(n). Give each complexity.
Show answer
f is O(n). g calls an O(i) function n times: 1 + 2 + … + n, so O(n²). h is O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.6 Six-step method: cost the innermost operation first, then work outwards; a call to a function adds that function’s cost.

Step 1. f(n) loops from 1 to n−1 doing a constant amount of work: n − 1 steps, O(n).

Step 2. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and in each pass calls f(i), which costs i steps. Total = 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2, so O(n²).

Step 3. h(n) = f(n) + g(n): the two run one after the other, so add: O(n) + O(n²). Keep the larger: O(n²).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q5

Cost of a nested call

func_a has two nested loops of size n and calls f(j) inside. What is its complexity if f costs a constant T, and if f(j) costs j time units?
Show answer
Constant T: n² · T = O(n²). Linear f(j) = j: n · (0 + 1 + … + (n−1)) = n · n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.6–2.7: nested loops multiply the body cost; the body cost may itself depend on the loop variable.

Step 1. Two nested loops of size n run the body n × n = n² times.

Step 2. If the body f(j) costs a constant T, total = n² × T, so O(n²).

Step 3. If f(j) costs j steps, the inner loop over j adds 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 for one pass of the outer loop. The outer loop repeats this n times: n × n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).

sub_func(n) is called inside: func_6a (for i in range(n), for j in range(i)); func_6b (for i in 1..n, for j in 1..i²); func_2c (for i, for j, if j % i == 0, for k in 1..n).
Show answer
The answer key gives O(n³), O(n⁴) and O(n³ log n), which is what you get when sub_func(n) costs O(n): 6a runs it n(n−1)/2 times; 6b runs it Σi² ≈ n³/3 times; in 2c the if is true about n/i times per i, a harmonic sum n log n, and each hit runs n calls of cost n.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns + §2.6 treat each helper call as a block of known cost (the key assumes sub_func(n) costs O(n)).

Step 1. func_6a: j runs from 0 to i−1, so the call happens 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 times. Each call costs n, so n × n(n−1)/2 ≈ n³/2: O(n³).

Step 2. func_6b: j runs 1 to i², so the call happens Σ i² ≈ n³/3 times, each costing n: n⁴/3, O(n⁴).

Step 3. func_2c: for each i, the if j % i == 0 is true about n/i times (the multiples of i up to n). Across i that is n(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …) ≈ n ln n hits (a harmonic sum). Each hit runs a loop of n calls costing n each: n² per hit, so total ≈ n log n × n²: O(n³ log n).

Check / common slip. Always state what cost you assume for the helper; if sub_func were O(1) every answer would drop by a factor of n.

IN-CLASS · Q1

First index with a[index] ≥ key

Correct first_at_least(a, key) so it returns the first index where a[index] ≥ key, or None. Trace keys 8, 20 and 40 on a = [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] and state time and space.
Show answer
Keep ans. If a[mid] >= key, save ans = mid and search left (high = mid − 1); otherwise low = mid + 1. Return ans after the loop. Results: key 8 gives index 1; key 20 gives index 5 (a[5] = 27, a[4] = 19); key 40 gives None because ans is never updated. Time O(log n), space O(1). The original bug moved right after a valid value and returned an index even when nothing qualified.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.3 Binary search and §3.1 loop invariant: “ans is the smallest index so far with a[ans] ≥ key; everything left of low is < key”.

Step 1. Ordinary binary search stops when it finds the key. Here we want the first index with a[index] ≥ key, so a hit is not final: a smaller index might also qualify. So when a[mid] ≥ key, record ans = mid and keep searching left (high = mid − 1). When a[mid] < key, mid and everything left of it fail: low = mid + 1.

Step 2. Trace key 8 on [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] (low 0, high 6): mid 3 → 14 ≥ 8, ans = 3, high = 2. mid 1 → 8 ≥ 8, ans = 1, high = 0. mid 0 → 3 < 8, low = 1. low > high, stop: 1.

Step 3. Key 20: mid 3 → 14 < 20, low = 4. mid 5 → 27 ≥ 20, ans = 5, high = 4. mid 4 → 19 < 20, low = 5. Stop: 5. Key 40: every probe says “<”, low runs off the end, ans never set: None.

Step 4. Each loop halves the range: time O(log n); only a few variables: space O(1).

Check / common slip. The original bug returned at the first hit (not necessarily the first index) and returned an index even when no value qualified. Initialise ans = None.

IN-CLASS · Q2

Run-length encoding in one pass

Convert [4, 4, 4, 7, 7, 2, 2, 2, 2, 9] into [(4, 3), (7, 2), (2, 4), (9, 1)], handling empty input and explaining the final append.
Show answer
State: value, count, out. Start value, count = a[0], 1. Equal next item: count += 1. Different: append (value, count) and restart. A run is appended only when a change is seen, so the last run must be appended once after the loop. Time O(n), working space O(1), output space O(r) for r runs.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.1 Reasoning about iterative algorithms: choose state variables, say what each means at the top of every pass (the invariant).

Step 1. State: value (the current run’s item), count (its length so far), out (finished runs). Initialise from a[0] (after checking the list is not empty, otherwise return []).

Step 2. For each next item x: if x equals value, the run continues, so count += 1. If not, the run just ended: append (value, count) and start a new run value = x, count = 1.

Step 3. A run is only appended when the next item differs. The last run has no next item, so nothing triggers its append: you must append it once after the loop.

Step 4. On [4,4,4,7,7,2,2,2,2,9] the changes are at 7, 2 and 9, giving (4,3), (7,2), (2,4) and then (9,1) from the final append. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) working space.

IN-CLASS · Q3

Merge two sorted arrays, keeping duplicates

Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], taking from A first on a tie.

Compare A[i] with B[j]; take A[i] when A[i] <= B[j], else B[j]; advance only the index used; copy leftovers. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. At most n + m values are appended: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) output space.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.6 Merge: two sorted piles, repeatedly take the smaller front card, then copy whatever is left.

Step 1. Keep pointers i on A and j on B. Compare A[i] and B[j]; take A[i] if A[i] ≤ B[j] (this tie rule keeps duplicates from A first), else take B[j]. Move only the pointer you used.

Step 2. A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31], B = [4, 9, 12, 28]: 2 (A) · 4 (B) · 9 (A, tie goes to A) · 9 (B) · 12 (B) · 15 (A) · 23 (A) · 28 (B) · B is empty, copy the leftover 31.

Step 3. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. Every value is appended once: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) space for the output.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Count inversions with nested loops

For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5], compare every pair i < j and count the pairs with a[i] > a[j].
Show answer
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 so each pair is compared once. Inversions: (7,2), (7,6), (7,3), (7,5), (6,3), (6,5), so the count is 6. Comparisons n(n−1)/2, time O(n²), working space O(1).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns (dependent inner loop) and §3.1 (what the loop covers).

Step 1. To compare each pair exactly once, start the inner loop at j = i + 1 (a pair (i, j) with i < j).

Step 2. For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5] list the pairs where the left value is bigger: 7 with 2, 6, 3, 5 (4 pairs); 2 with none; 6 with 3, 5 (2 pairs); 3 with 5 none. Total 6.

Step 3. There are n(n−1)/2 pairs checked, so time O(n²), space O(1).

IN-CLASS · Q5

Search a row-and-column sorted matrix

Start at the top-right cell and find 13. Move left when the current value is larger than the target and down when it is smaller.
Show answer
If the current value is too large, its whole column below is larger, so move left. If it is too small, its whole row to the left is smaller, so move down. For target 13 the path is 18, 10, 15, 9, 13, found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based). Each comparison discards a row or column: at most r + c − 1 checks, O(r + c) time, O(1) space.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.3 (discard a part that cannot hold the target) applied in two dimensions; §3.1 invariant: “if the target is in the matrix it is in the remaining rows and columns”.

Step 1. Start at the top-right cell. In a matrix sorted along every row (left to right) and down every column, that cell is the largest in its row and the smallest in its column.

Step 2. If the current value is larger than the target, nothing below it in this column can help (everything below is even larger), so discard the column: move left. If it is smaller, nothing to its left in this row can help, so discard the row: move down.

Step 3. Target 13: 18 (too big, left) → 10 (too small, down) → 15 (too big, left) → 9 (too small, down) → 13 found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based).

Step 4. Every comparison removes a row or a column, so at most r + c − 1 checks: O(r + c) time, O(1) space.

TUTORIAL 3 · TIER 1 · Q2

Modify linear search for duplicates

Return (a) the number of occurrences of k, (b) the index of the second occurrence or None, (c) the index of the last occurrence or None.
Show answer
(a) Do not return inside the loop; keep count += 1 and return count after it. (b) Increment count on a match and return i when count == 2; otherwise None. (c) Remember the latest matching index in last_index and return it after the loop, or scan from the back and return the first match.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.2 Linear search: you may keep scanning instead of returning at the first match.

Step 1. (a) Count: do not return inside the loop. Add 1 to count for every match and return count after the loop.

Step 2. (b) Second occurrence: on each match increase count; when count reaches 2 return the current index i. If the loop ends without that, return None.

Step 3. (c) Last occurrence: remember the latest matching index in last_index (overwrite each time) and return it after the loop, or scan from the back and return the first match.

TUTORIAL 3 · TIER 1 · Q3

Insertion sort, descending

Change the insertion sort to sort in descending order. What are its best and worst cases?
Show answer
Change the shifting condition to while position > 0 and value > list[position-1]. Best case O(n) when the input is already in descending order. Worst case O(n²) when it is in ascending order.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.5 Insertion sort: the left part is sorted; shift bigger-than-value items one place right until the value fits. The shifting condition defines the order.

Step 1. Ascending uses while position > 0 and list[position−1] > value (shift larger items). To sort descending, flip the comparison: shift items that are smaller than the value, i.e. while position > 0 and value > list[position−1].

Step 2. Best case: the input is already in the desired order (here descending). Every value fails the while test immediately: one comparison per item, O(n).

Step 3. Worst case: the input is in the opposite order (ascending). Each value must shift past all earlier items: 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) shifts, O(n²).

TUTORIAL 3 · TIER 1 · Q4

What does x look like just before the final merge for [96, 80, 88, 34, 47, 65, 52, 73], [62, 77, 18, 48, 64, 45, 34, 88, 82, 87, 17] and [27, 92, 93, 91, 35, 22, 31]?

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.6 Bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of width 1, then 2, 4, 8, …; a leftover short run is merged last.

Step 1. Bottom-up makes passes with run lengths 1, 2, 4, 8 … Just before the final merge there are two runs, and each is already sorted internally.

Step 2. 8 values: runs of 4 and 4. Sort each half: [96, 80, 88, 34] → [34, 80, 88, 96] and [47, 65, 52, 73] → [47, 52, 65, 73]. So x = [34, 80, 88, 96, 47, 52, 65, 73].

Step 3. 11 values: the last full pass makes a run of 8 and leaves 3: [62, 77, 18, 48, 64, 45, 34, 88] sorts to [18, 34, 45, 48, 62, 64, 77, 88]; [82, 87, 17] sorts to [17, 82, 87]. So x = [18, 34, 45, 48, 62, 64, 77, 88, 17, 82, 87].

Step 4. 7 values: runs of 4 and 3: [27, 92, 93, 91] → [27, 91, 92, 93]; [35, 22, 31] → [22, 31, 35].

TUTORIAL 3 · TIER 1 · Q5

Maximum of a shifted sorted array

A sorted array A is shifted right by k to give Aₖ. Find the maximum when k is known in O(1), when k is unknown in O(N), and when k is unknown in O(log N).
Show answer
Known k: the original maximum at index n−1 moves to ((n−1) + k) % n = (k−1) % n, so read that index in O(1). Unknown k, O(N): linear scan until an element is larger than its right neighbour. Unknown k, O(log N): binary search; if the middle element is bigger than the one to its right, it is the maximum, otherwise move toward the side that contains the break.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.3 Binary search idea: compare the middle with a neighbour to decide which half holds the break.

Step 1. A sorted array shifted right by k has its largest value (originally at index n−1) at index (n − 1 + k) mod n.

Step 2. k known, O(1): read that index directly.

Step 3. k unknown, O(N): scan; the maximum is the item that is bigger than the item to its right (the break point).

Step 4. k unknown, O(log N): binary search on the break: if A[mid] > A[mid+1], A[mid] is the maximum. Otherwise compare A[mid] with A[0]: if A[mid] ≥ A[0] the break is to the right, so move low = mid + 1; else it is to the left, so high = mid. Each step halves the range.

TUTORIAL 3 · TIER 1 · Q6

Find the missing integer

B holds n distinct integers from 1 to n + 1 with exactly one missing. Find it with the lowest complexity.
Show answer
Four approaches in the answer key: search for each number in turn, O(n²); sort then find the gap, O(n log n); compare the sum with 1 + 2 + … + (n+1), O(n) time and O(1) space; or a flag array, O(n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.2 Why count growth: compare candidate algorithms by their cost, then pick the cheapest.

Step 1. Search each number from 1 to n+1 in B: n+1 searches × O(n) each = O(n²). Easy but slow.

Step 2. Sort B (O(n log n)), then scan for the first position where B[i] ≠ i+1: O(n log n).

Step 3. Use arithmetic: the full sum 1 + … + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2. Subtract the sum of B: the difference is the missing number. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space: the best.

Step 4. Or mark seen values in a flag array of size n+1 and report the unmarked one: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Check / common slip. The “lowest complexity” answer is the sum trick; the exam wants you to name the approach and its cost.

IN-CLASS · Q1

Cost of power1

power1(x, n) returns 1 when n == 0, otherwise x * power1(x, n-1). How many multiplications for x = 3, n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
16 multiplications, one per call down to n = 0. Complexity O(n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.1 Recursion: a call on a smaller input plus one multiplication; §4.3 count calls by tracing down to the base case.

Step 1. power1(3, 16) = 3 × power1(3, 15) = 3 × 3 × power1(3, 14) = … Each call reduces n by exactly 1 and does one multiplication.

Step 2. The chain of calls is n = 16, 15, …, 1, 0. The base case n = 0 does no multiplication; every other call (16 of them) does one: 16 multiplications.

Step 3. The work grows linearly with n: O(n).

IN-CLASS · Q2

Cost of power2

power2(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; for even n it returns power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2); for odd n it returns x * power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2). How many multiplications for n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
Two recursive calls per level, so the instances double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 at n = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0. Multiplications: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16×2 + 32×0 = 47. An odd n costs 2 multiplications, an even n costs 1, and n = 0 costs 0. In general at most 2(n−1) + 2n multiplications, so O(n). Calling the halved problem once and reusing the result (power3) removes the doubling.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.5 Halving is not automatically O(log n): what counts is how many calls are made at each level.

Step 1. power2(x, n) halves n but calls itself twice. So the number of instances doubles each level while n halves.

Step 2. Levels: n = 16 (1 instance), 8 (2 instances), 4 (4), 2 (8), 1 (16), 0 (32). The base case does nothing.

Step 3. Multiplications per instance: an even n costs 1 (the product of the two results), an odd n costs 2 (x × a × b). So: 1 (n=16) + 2 × 1 (n=8) + 4 × 1 (n=4) + 8 × 1 (n=2) + 16 × 2 (n=1) = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 32 = 47.

Step 4. The number of instances grows like n, so the total is proportional to n: O(n). The halving was cancelled by the doubling.

Check / common slip. Fix: compute the half-power once, store it in a variable, and reuse it: that is power3, exercise 5 of the tutorial.

For [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5] and [52, 30, 98, 59, 67, 4, 64, 12, 79], give the array just before the final merge for the bottom-up and top-down versions.

The two versions reach different intermediate states, so say which version you are tracing.

Step 1. Top-down on [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5]: mid = 3 gives halves [26, 34, 64] and [83, 2, 5]. Each half is sorted completely before the final merge: [26, 34, 64] and [2, 5, 83]. Array before final merge: [26, 34, 64, 2, 5, 83].

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q1

Pascal triangle recursion

Complete pt(n, k), where pt(n, k) = pt(n−1, k−1) + pt(n−1, k) and the first and last entries of each level are 1. Then trace pt(4, 2).
Show answer
if k == 1: return 1; if k == n + 1: return 1; return pt(n-1, k-1) + pt(n-1, k). pt(4, 2) = pt(3, 1) + pt(3, 2) = 1 + (pt(2, 1) + pt(2, 2)) = 1 + (1 + 2) = 4.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.1 Recursion needs base cases and a smaller call; Pascal’s rule gives the combination step.

Step 1. Base cases: the first entry (k == 1) and the last entry (k == n + 1) of each row are 1. Otherwise each entry is the sum of the two above it: pt(n−1, k−1) + pt(n−1, k).

Step 2. Trace pt(4, 2) = pt(3, 1) + pt(3, 2). pt(3, 1) is a base case: 1. pt(3, 2) = pt(2, 1) + pt(2, 2) = 1 + 2, where pt(2, 2) = pt(1, 1) + pt(1, 2) = 1 + 1 = 2.

Step 3. So pt(4, 2) = 1 + (1 + 2) = 4. This is the second entry of row 4, which equals C(4, 1).

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q2

power3 with one recursive call

power3(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; otherwise it computes temp = power3(x, n//2) and returns temp * temp for even n, or x * temp * temp for odd n. How many multiplications for x = 3 with n = 16 and n = 19, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
n = 16: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6. n = 19: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8. There are up to log₂ n + 1 instances with at most 2 multiplications each, so O(log n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.5 Halving: one recursive call per level gives O(log n); the fix for power2 is to save the result of the single call.

Step 1. temp = power3(x, n // 2) is computed once. Then even n returns temp × temp (1 multiplication), odd n returns x × temp × temp (2 multiplications).

Step 2. n = 16: calls at n = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0. Even n = 16, 8, 4, 2 give 1 each = 4. n = 1 is odd: 2. n = 0: none. Total 4 + 2 = 6.

Step 3. n = 19: n = 19 (odd, 2), 9 (odd, 2), 4 (even, 1), 2 (even, 1), 1 (odd, 2), 0 (none): 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8.

Step 4. The chain length is about log₂n + 1 and each level does at most 2 multiplications: O(log n).

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q3

Recursive calls with a linear helper

sub_function is linear. What is the complexity of my_function(n) when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n//2); when it calls sub_function(k) with my_function(k, n//2); and when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n-1)?
Show answer
O(n): n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n. O(k log n): log n levels, each costing O(k). O(n²): n + (n−1) + … + 1.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.6 Recurrences: write T(n) as the work of this call plus the work of the recursive calls, then unroll.

Step 1. T(n) = n + T(n/2): n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n, a geometric series that stays proportional to n: O(n).

Step 2. T(n) = k + T(n/2) where the helper costs k (a fixed amount): k is paid on each of the log₂n levels: O(k log n).

Step 3. T(n) = n + T(n−1): n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2: O(n²).

Check / common slip. The difference between the first and third is how fast the argument shrinks. Halving makes the series geometric; subtracting 1 makes it an arithmetic series.

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q4

Recursive maximum

Write a recursive max_array(a) without sorting.
Show answer
Slicing version: if len(a) == 1: return a[0], otherwise return max(a[0], max_array(a[1:])). A faster-copying version passes lower and upper: base cases when the range is empty or has one value, otherwise mid = (lower + upper) // 2 and return max(max_array(a, lower, mid), max_array(a, mid, upper)). Both are O(n) in the worst case, since every element must be examined.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.1–4.2 Three safety questions: base case? smaller input? does the combination give the right answer?

Step 1. Base case: a one-element list: its maximum is that element.

Step 2. Smaller input: drop the first element: a[1:]. Combination: the maximum of the whole list is max(a[0], maximum of the rest).

Step 3. Code: if len(a) == 1: return a[0]; return max(a[0], max_array(a[1:])).

Step 4. Every element must be looked at, so O(n) comparisons (slicing copies add extra cost; the lower/upper version passes indices to avoid that).

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q5

Recursive palindrome

Write a recursive is_palindrome(s).
Show answer
Compare the first and last characters. Base cases: length 0 or 1 gives True; a mismatch gives False. Otherwise recurse on s[1:len(s)-1]. An index version keeps i and stops when i > len(s) − 1 − i. Worst case O(n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.1–4.2 Reduce the problem from both ends: peel off the first and last characters.

Step 1. Base cases: length 0 or 1 is a palindrome (True). If the first and last characters differ, it is not a palindrome (False).

Step 2. Otherwise the string is a palindrome exactly when the middle part (without first and last) is: recurse on s[1:len(s)−1].

Step 3. Each call shortens the string by 2 and does constant comparison work (ignoring the slice copying): O(n) in the worst case.

TUTORIAL 4 · TIER 1 · Q6

Sign-alternating recurrence

f(n) returns 1 for n 0 or 1, otherwise −f(n−1) − f(n−2). Give f(1), f(5), f(6), f(330) and the worst-case complexity.
Show answer
f(1) = 1, f(5) = −2, f(6) = 1, f(330) = 1 (the values repeat with period 3: 1, 1, −2). Each call makes two calls on n−1 and n−2, so the worst case is exponential, about O(1.6ⁿ) or O(2ⁿ).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.4 Branching recursion: compute small values first and find the pattern; §4.6 two recursive calls means exponential growth.

Step 1. f(0) = f(1) = 1. f(2) = −f(1) − f(0) = −2. f(3) = −f(2) − f(1) = 2 − 1 = 1. f(4) = −f(3) − f(2) = −1 + 2 = 1. f(5) = −f(4) − f(3) = −2. f(6) = −f(5) − f(4) = 2 − 1 = 1.

Step 2. The values repeat 1, 1, −2, 1, 1, −2, … with period 3: f(n) = 1 unless n mod 3 = 2, when it is −2. So f(1) = 1, f(5) = −2, f(6) = 1, and f(330) = 1 because 330 mod 3 = 0.

Step 3. Each call spawns calls on n−1 and n−2, like naive Fibonacci: the call tree has about 1.6ⁿ nodes: exponential, written O(2ⁿ). (Memoisation would make it O(n).)

IN-CLASS · Q1

Browser back, forward and visit

Stacks U = [C, B, A] (C on top), current page D, R empty. Run: back, back, forward, visit(E), back. Record U, current page and R after each action.
Show answer
Start: U [C, B, A], current D, R []. back: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. back: U [A], current B, R [C, D]. forward: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. visit(E): U [C, B, A], current E, R [] (visit clears R). back: U [B, A], current C, R [E]. Forward is available because R is not empty and holds E.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.3 Stack: push puts on top, pop takes the top. A browser is two stacks and a “current page”.

Step 1. Name the three pieces: U = pages you can go back to (top = most recent), current page, R = pages you can go forward to.

Step 2. Write the rule for each action. back: push the current page onto R, then pop U to become the current page. forward: push the current page onto U, then pop R. visit(x): push the current page onto U, make x current, and empty R (the old “future” no longer exists).

Step 3. Trace. Start U [C, B, A], current D, R []. back: R [D], current C, U [B, A]. back: R [C, D], current B, U [A]. forward: pop R gives C, push B onto U: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. visit(E): push C onto U → U [C, B, A], current E, R cleared []. back: R [E], current C, U [B, A].

Check / common slip. Each page stays in exactly one of U, current or R. If you lose a page in your trace, a push or pop was skipped.

IN-CLASS · Q2

Round-robin help desk

Queue [(A, 5), (B, 2), (C, 4)], head first. Each turn dequeues the head, processes min(2, remaining) minutes, then finishes the job or enqueues it at the tail. Give the completion order and number of turns.
Show answer
Turn 1: A 5 to 3, queue [B2, C4, A3]. Turn 2: B finishes. Turn 3: C 4 to 2, queue [A3, C2]. Turn 4: A 3 to 1, queue [C2, A1]. Turn 5: C finishes. Turn 6: A finishes. Completion order B, C, A in 6 turns. In general the turns equal Σ ⌈tᵢ/2⌉ and the number of queue operations is O(Σ tᵢ) for a fixed quantum.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.4 Queue: the head is served and, if unfinished, rejoins the tail.

Step 1. Rule per turn: dequeue the head, give it min(2, remaining) minutes, then either it is finished (leaves for good) or enqueue it at the tail with its new remaining time.

Step 2. Turn 1: A(5) → 3 left, queue [B2, C4, A3]. Turn 2: B(2) → 0, finished; queue [C4, A3]. Turn 3: C(4) → 2, queue [A3, C2]. Turn 4: A(3) → 1, queue [C2, A1]. Turn 5: C(2) → 0 finished; queue [A1]. Turn 6: A(1) → 0 finished.

Step 3. Completion order B, C, A, 6 turns. Count check: each job needs ⌈time/2⌉ turns: 3 + 1 + 2 = 6.

IN-CLASS · Q3

Remove adjacent duplicates

Process ABBACA left to right with a stack: pop if the character equals the top, otherwise push.
Show answer
Stack after each character: [A], [A, B], [A] (second B cancels), [] (A cancels), [C], [C, A]. Final string, bottom to top: CA. Removing one pair can expose a new equal pair underneath, which the stack handles automatically. Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.3 Stack: the top is the only element you can compare with, so the newest character is always the one to cancel.

Step 1. For each character: if the stack is not empty and the top equals the character, pop (the pair cancels). Otherwise push it.

Step 2. A → [A]. B → [A, B]. B equals the top, pop → [A]. A equals the top, pop → []. C → [C]. A → [C, A].

Step 3. Read the stack bottom to top: CA. The second A cancelled the first A only because removing BB had made them adjacent, which a stack handles automatically.

Check / common slip. Doing it by scanning the string repeatedly also works but needs many passes. The stack does it in one pass: O(n) time.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Priority help desk

Smaller number is higher priority; ties go to the earlier arrival. Start with A(3), B(1), C(2). Perform: enqueue D(1); dequeue; enqueue E(2); dequeue; dequeue.
Show answer
After enqueue D(1): next order B, D, C, A. Dequeue returns B. Enqueue E(2): order D, C, E, A. Dequeue returns D. Dequeue returns C. The remaining queue is E(2), A(3), so the complete removal sequence is B, D, C, E, A.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.5 Priority queue: dequeue returns the best priority (smallest number); equal priorities are served by arrival.

Step 1. Keep the waiting list sorted by (priority, arrival). Start: B1, C2, A3.

Step 2. enqueue D(1): sorted order B1, D1 (B arrived first), C2, A3. dequeue → B.

Step 3. enqueue E(2): D1, C2, E2 (C arrived before E), A3. dequeue → D. dequeue → C. Left: E2, A3.

Step 4. Full removal sequence B, D, C, E, A. Note A arrived first of all but is served last: it has the worst priority.

IN-CLASS · Q5

Queue from two stacks

enqueue pushes onto IN. dequeue pops OUT, but if OUT is empty it first moves every IN value onto OUT. Trace: enqueue A, B, C, dequeue, enqueue D, dequeue, dequeue, enqueue E, dequeue.
Show answer
Enqueues leave IN [A, B, C]. First dequeue transfers, so OUT [C, B] after returning A. Enqueue D gives IN [D]. Dequeue returns B, then C (OUT empties). Enqueue E gives IN [D, E]. The last dequeue transfers and returns D, leaving OUT [E], so the next item is E. One dequeue is O(n) in the worst case (a transfer), but each element moves at most once, so the amortised cost is O(1) per operation. Auxiliary space O(n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.3–5.4: reversing the order of a stack twice restores it; a queue made from two stacks pays a transfer only when OUT is empty.

Step 1. IN receives every enqueue. OUT serves every dequeue. When OUT is empty, move all of IN across one by one: the order reverses, so the oldest item ends up on top of OUT.

Step 2. enqueue A, B, C: IN [A, B, C], OUT []. dequeue: OUT is empty, transfer: pop C, B, A and push them → OUT [C, B, A] (A on top); pop A: returns A, OUT [C, B].

Step 3. enqueue D: IN [D]. dequeue: OUT not empty, pop B (B). dequeue: pop C (C), OUT empty. enqueue E: IN [D, E]. dequeue: OUT empty, transfer: OUT [E, D], pop D: D, OUT [E].

Step 4. Order out: A, B, C, D, with E next, which is exactly the order in (FIFO).

Step 5. Cost: one dequeue can cost O(n) (a transfer), but every element is moved at most once from IN to OUT, so n operations cost O(n) in total: O(1) amortised.

[4, 4, 7], with 4 at the head. Trace: [0], [1], [1, 2], [2, 4], [2, 4, 4], [4, 4, 7].

TUTORIAL 5 · TIER 1 · Q3

Which pop sequences are possible?

Numbers 1 to n are pushed in increasing order, with pops at any time. Give operations that print 1 3 5 4 2. Is there a sequence that cannot occur?
Show answer
Push 1, pop (1); push 2, push 3, pop (3); push 4, push 5, pop (5), pop (4), pop (2). Impossible example: 1 5 4 2 3. Once a value n₃ is popped, two smaller values that were pushed earlier cannot come out in increasing order, so 3, 1, 2 can never occur.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.3 Stack: items come out in reverse of the order they went in, unless they are popped earlier.

Step 1. Target output 1 3 5 4 2 with pushes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order. Process the output one number at a time: push numbers until the wanted one is on top, then pop it.

Step 2. Want 1: push 1, pop (1). Want 3: push 2, push 3, pop (3); 2 stays inside. Want 5: push 4, push 5, pop (5). Want 4: it is on top, pop (4). Want 2: it is on top, pop (2).

Step 3. Impossible sequences exist. For 3 1 2: to pop 3 first you must have pushed 1, 2, 3, so the stack is 1 (bottom), 2, 3 (top). After popping 3 the top is 2, so 2 must come out before 1: the output 3 1 2 can never occur. For 1 5 4 2 3: after 1, popping 5 requires pushing 2, 3, 4, 5; after 5 and 4 the stack is 2 (bottom), 3 (top), so 3 must come out before 2, and the sequence ending 2 3 is impossible.

Check / common slip. A quick test for a candidate sequence: simulate it with a stack; if you ever need a number that is buried under another, it is impossible.

TUTORIAL 5 · TIER 1 · Q4

Invert, and delete, using the other structure

Invert a queue using a stack; invert a stack using a queue; delete one element from a stack using a queue while keeping the rest in order.
Show answer
Invert the queue: dequeue everything onto the stack, then pop everything back into the queue. Invert the stack: pop everything into the queue, then dequeue everything back onto the stack. Delete from the stack: pop each element into the queue unless it is the one to delete; push everything back (now reversed); pop into the queue again; push back (original order restored without the deleted element).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.3 + §5.4: reversing is what a stack does naturally; a queue keeps order. Compose them.

Step 1. Invert a queue [1, 2, 3] using a stack: dequeue each into the stack (stack bottom to top: 1, 2, 3), then pop each back into the queue: 3, 2, 1. The queue is now [3, 2, 1].

Step 2. Invert a stack using a queue: pop each into the queue (the top comes out first, so the queue is top, …, bottom), then dequeue each back onto the stack: the old top is pushed first and ends at the bottom. Stack reversed.

Step 3. Delete one element x from a stack, keeping the rest in order: pop each element into the queue except x (throw x away). Push everything back: the stack is now reversed. Pop all into the queue again, push all back: reversed twice means the original order, minus x.

TUTORIAL 5 · TIER 1 · Q5

Non-recursive factorial

Convert the recursive factorial into a version that uses a stack.
Show answer
Push n; result = 1; while the stack is not empty, pop m, result *= m, and if m > 1 push m − 1. Return result.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §5.6 Link back to recursion: a stack plays the part of the call stack; each pop is “finishing the newest unfinished call”.

Step 1. The recursive version factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1) first goes down n, n−1, …, 1 and then multiplies on the way back. Replace the call stack with an explicit stack.

Step 2. Push n. Keep result = 1. While the stack is not empty: pop m, multiply result by m, and if m > 1, push m − 1 (the smaller problem).

Step 3. Trace n = 4: stack [4] → pop 4, result 4, push 3 → pop 3, result 12, push 2 → pop 2, result 24, push 1 → pop 1, result 24, nothing pushed → stack empty. Return 24.

Cars BST: insertion order against alphabetical order

Insert Lexus, Mercedes, BMW, Audi, Lamborghini, Chevrolet, Porsche, Maserati, Lotus into a BST in that order. Count comparisons to find Audi, Lamborghini, Maserati and Porsche. Repeat when inserting in alphabetical order.

Step 1. Insert in the listed order. Lexus is the root. Mercedes > Lexus: right. BMW < Lexus: left. Audi < Lexus, < BMW: left of BMW. Lamborghini < Lexus, > BMW: right of BMW. Badminton tournament

Round 1: 7 games; round 2: 3; round 3: 2; round 4: 1. Total 13 games. In general n − 1 games, so O(n) (13 people need 12 games, 12 people need 11).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §6.1 Tree reasoning: a tournament is a tree where every game removes exactly one player.

Step 1. Count by rounds. 14 players: 7 games, 7 winners. 7 players: 3 games and 1 gets a bye (promoted automatically): 4 left. 4 players: 2 games: 2 left. Final: 1 game. Total 7 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 13.

Step 2. Shortcut by invariant: each game eliminates exactly one player and the tournament ends with exactly one left, so there are always n − 1 games (14 → 13).

Step 3. So the complexity is O(n).

TUTORIAL 6 · TIER 1 · Q4

TreeSort

Insert each element into a BST, then traverse to print in sorted order. Which traversal, and what is the worst-case complexity?
Show answer
In-order traversal. Inserting n elements costs O(n²) in the worst case (a chain) and the traversal costs O(n), so the overall worst case is O(n²).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §6.3 Traversals: in-order on a BST visits keys in increasing order; §6.5 cost of building depends on the shape.

Step 1. TreeSort: insert every element into a BST, then print by in-order traversal (left, node, right). In-order of a BST is sorted by definition of the BST property.

Step 2. Cost: inserting n elements costs the depth of each insertion. If the tree is balanced, about log n each: O(n log n). In the worst case (already sorted input) the tree is a chain and the k-th insertion costs k: 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²). The traversal itself costs O(n).

Step 3. Worst case overall: O(n²).

TUTORIAL 6 · TIER 1 · Q5

Could this array be a BST postorder?

Design an algorithm that returns True if an array of distinct numbers could be the postorder traversal of some BST, and give its worst-case complexity.
Show answer
Brute force: try every permutation as an insertion order and compare postorders, O(n! · n²). Better: the last element is the root. Find a split point so everything before it is smaller than the root and everything after is larger, then check both parts recursively; no split point means False. Worst case O(n²). Another way: reverse the array, insert it into a BST (O(n²)), take the postorder (O(n)), and compare with the input.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §6.3 Postorder visits left subtree, right subtree, then the node, so the last element must be the root; §6.4 the BST rule says left keys < root < right keys.

Step 1. Brute force: try every ordering of the numbers as an insertion order, build each BST, compare its postorder to the array: n! orderings × O(n²) each = O(n!·n²).

Step 2. Better: the last element r is the root. Scan from the start: the leading values smaller than r should form the left subtree and all the rest (up to r) must be larger than r for the right subtree. Find the first value bigger than r: that is the split. If any later value in the right part is smaller than r, answer False.

Step 3. Recurse on the left part and the right part (each of them has its own last element as root). If no violation is found anywhere, answer True.

Step 4. Each level scans its part once, and the recursion depth can be n in a skewed tree: worst case O(n²).

TUTORIAL 6 · TIER 1 · Q6

BST from an array and traversals

Build the BST by inserting A = [2, 10, 4, 7, 19, 5, 8, 11, 3, 15] left to right. Give the preorder and postorder traversals, then reorder A into B so that the BST has the worst-case chain shape.

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §6.4 BST insertion + §6.3 Traversals + §6.5 shape.

Step 1. Insert A = [2, 10, 4, 7, 19, 5, 8, 11, 3, 15] one by one: 2 is the root. 10 right of 2. 4: >2, <10: left of 10. 7: >2, <10, >4: right of 4. 19: right of 10. 5: >4, <7: left of 7. 8: >7: right of 7. 11: >10, <19: left of 19. 3: <4: left of 4. 15: >11: right of 11.

Step 2. Preorder (node, left, right): 2, 10, 4, 3, 7, 5, 8, 19, 11, 15. Postorder (left, right, node): 3, 5, 8, 7, 4, 15, 11, 19, 10, 2.

Step 3. Worst case shape = every new key becomes a child of the previous deepest node (a chain). Sorted order does this (always right). The answer key uses a zig-zag order, B = [2, 19, 3, 15, 4, 11, 5, 10, 7, 8]: smallest, largest, second smallest, second largest, … so each key lands below the previous one but alternating left/right. Height n, so searching is O(n).

Step 2. Step 2: call removeMin k times. Each call is O(log N), so O(k log N).

Step 3. The removed numbers come out smallest first, so after k calls you hold the k smallest. Total O(N + k log N). If k = N this is O(N log N), the cost of heap sort.

Step 4. If you built the heap by N separate inserts instead, step 1 costs O(N log N), so the total is O(N log N + k log N): never better than buildHeap.

In the tutorial example, repeated insertion needed 9 swaps and gave [27, 39, 65, 43, 44, 88, 82, 83, 45, 79], while bottom-up buildHeap needed 7 swaps and gave [27, 39, 65, 43, 44, 82, 88, 45, 83, 79]. Bottom-up construction is O(n) while repeated insertion is O(n log n).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §7.6 BuildHeap: sink every parent from the last parent back to the root; §7.3 inserting one by one bubbles each new value up its full path.

Step 1. Count a swap each time a value exchanges place with a parent or child.

Step 2. Illustration on [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] (any decreasing input shows the idea). Insert one by one: insert 4 swaps past 5 (1), 3 swaps past 4 (1), 2 swaps twice (2), 1 swaps twice (2): 6 swaps, giving [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Bottom-up buildHeap: the last parent is index 1 (value 4): it swaps with its smaller child 1 (1 swap); then index 0 (value 5) sinks past 1 and then 2 (2 swaps): 3 swaps, giving [1, 2, 3, 5, 4].

Step 3. For the tutorial sequence the same comparison gave 9 swaps for repeated insertion and 7 for buildHeap: apply the procedure by hand and count swaps in each.

Step 4. Why buildHeap needs fewer: half of the nodes are leaves and need no work; a node near the bottom sinks only a step or two. Inserting bubbles every new value up through up to log n levels, and half the values land near the bottom. Overall: O(n) versus O(n log n).

TUTORIAL 7 · Q3

A legal but poor hash code

Is a hash_code() that gives every key the same value legal? Describe the effect.
Show answer
It is legal, but inappropriate: all keys land in the same cell, so the table degenerates into an unsorted table map and a search takes O(n) in the worst case.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §8.2 Hash functions: a hash code only has to be deterministic (same key → same value) to be legal; §8.3 the quality is how well it spreads keys.

Step 1. A function that returns the same number for every key is deterministic, so a table will still work: it is legal.

Step 2. But every key is sent to the same row. With chaining, every key sits in one chain; with probing, every key probes the same long run. A lookup walks through up to all n entries: O(n), no better than scanning an unsorted list.

Step 3. So it is legal but inappropriate: a good hash function must also spread keys roughly uniformly across the table.

TUTORIAL 7 · Q4

Two numbers that sum to x

Design an algorithm that takes O(n) on average to decide whether an array of n numbers has two elements whose sum is a given x. Consider a hash map.
Show answer
Store the elements in a hash map. For each element a, check whether x − a is already in the map (an O(1) average lookup). Return True when found; otherwise add a and continue. One pass, O(n) on average.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §8.2–8.4: a hash map answers “have I seen this key?” in O(1) on average, which turns a double loop into a single pass.

Step 1. Brute force would check every pair: n² pairs. Instead, for each element a we only need to know whether x − a has already appeared.

Step 2. Keep a hash map of values seen so far. For each a: look up x − a (O(1) average). If present, the pair exists: return True. Otherwise insert a and move on.

Step 3. One pass, n lookups and n inserts at O(1) average each: O(n) average. Example: x = 9, array [3, 5, 4, 6]: see 3 (map {3}); see 5 (9−5 = 4 not in map; map {3,5}); see 4: 9−4 = 5 is in the map: True.

Check / common slip. Check x − a before inserting a, so an element is not paired with itself.

IN-CLASS · Q1

Represent a directed graph

Vertices A to F; edges in order A→B, A→C, B→D, C→B, C→E, D→E, E→C; F is isolated. Give the adjacency list, the degree table and the number of edges.
Show answer
Adjacency list: A [B, C], B [D], C [B, E], D [E], E [C], F []. In-degrees A0 B2 C2 D1 E2 F0 and out-degrees A2 B1 C2 D1 E1 F0. Both sums are 7, so there are 7 directed edges. The matrix has row = source and column = target, and F still gets a row and column of zeros.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §9.0–9.2 Representing a graph: the adjacency list stores, for each vertex, where its arrows go; degrees count arrows in and out.

Step 1. Go through the edge list in order and append the target to the source’s list: A→B, A→C gives A [B, C]. B→D gives B [D]. C→B, C→E gives C [B, E]. D→E gives D [E]. E→C gives E [C]. F has no edges: F [].

Step 2. Out-degree = length of the vertex’s own list: A2, B1, C2, D1, E1, F0. In-degree = how many lists contain that vertex: A appears in none (0); B in A and C (2); C in A and E (2); D in B (1); E in C and D (2); F in none (0).

Step 3. Each directed edge adds 1 to one out-degree and 1 to one in-degree, so both sums equal the number of edges: 2+1+2+1+1+0 = 7 and 0+2+2+1+2+0 = 7. So there are 7 edges.

Step 4. Matrix version: a 6 × 6 grid with a 1 in row source, column target for each of the 7 edges. F still gets a row and a column of zeros.

IN-CLASS · Q2

BFS and a fewest-edge route

Run BFS from A on that graph (mark on enqueue). Give the visit sequence, the unreached vertices, and a fewest-edge route from A to E.
Show answer
Queue: [A], then [B, C], [C, D], [D, E] (C adds E), [E] (D adds nothing: E is already marked), []. Visit sequence A, B, C, D, E. F is unreached because no edge leads into it. The fewest-edge route is A → C → E (2 edges), since BFS explores layer by layer and E first appears from C.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §9.3 BFS: a queue, mark a vertex visited the moment it is enqueued, take from the front.

Step 1. Start: mark A, queue [A].

Step 2. Dequeue A: neighbours B, C are new: mark and enqueue → [B, C]. Dequeue B: neighbour D is new → [C, D]. Dequeue C: its neighbours are B (visited) and E (new) → enqueue E → [D, E]. Dequeue D: neighbour E is already marked, nothing new → [E]. Dequeue E: neighbour C is visited → [].

Step 3. Visit sequence = order of marking: A, B, C, D, E. F never entered the queue because no edge leads into it: F is unreached.

Step 4. Route: BFS explores in layers (A, then B and C one edge away, then D and E two edges away). E first appears while dequeuing C, so E’s parent is C and the path back is E ← C ← A. Fewest-edge route A → C → E (2 edges).

IN-CLASS · Q3

Recursive DFS against stack DFS

Trace both DFS versions on the same graph from A. The stack version pushes neighbours in reverse list order and marks on pop.
Show answer
Recursive: A, B, D, E, C. Explicit stack: 6 pops, 5 new visits, visit sequence A, B, D, E, C. The extra pop is a duplicate C that was already visited, which is skipped (pending duplicates are allowed). The two sequences agree here, and F is unreached.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §9.4 DFS: recursion and an explicit stack do the same walk; the stack version pushes neighbours so the first in the list is explored first.

Step 1. Recursive: visit A; its first neighbour B: visit B; B’s first neighbour D: visit D; D’s neighbour E: visit E; E’s neighbour C: visit C; C’s neighbours B and E are visited, so C finishes, then E, D, B finish; A’s second neighbour C is already visited. Order A, B, D, E, C.

Step 2. Stack version (push neighbours in reverse list order, mark on pop): pop A visit, push C, B (stack C, B with B on top). Pop B visit, push D. Pop D visit, push E. Pop E visit, push C (stack C, C). Pop C visit (its neighbours are visited). Pop C again: already visited, discard.

Step 3. That is 6 pops, 5 visits, order A, B, D, E, C, same as the recursive version. The duplicate C on the stack is the price of marking on pop. F is unreached.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Topological order of a showcase plan

Adjacency lists A [C, D], B [D], C [E], D [E], E [], F []; outer loop order A to F; DFS-based method with a finish stack.
Show answer
Finish-stack pushes in order: E, C, D, A, B, F. Popping gives the order F, B, A, D, C, E. Every edge points forward. Of the proposed orders, A, B, C, D, E, F is valid, but A, C, D, B, E, F is not, because B must come before D (edge B → D). Adding E → A creates the cycle A → C → E → A, so no topological order exists.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §9.6 DAGs and topological sort: run DFS from every unvisited vertex in the given outer order; a vertex goes on the finish stack when everything it points to is finished; pop the stack for the order.

Step 1. Outer loop A, B, C, D, E, F. DFS(A): go to C (first neighbour), then C’s neighbour E. E has no out-edges: finish E. Back at C, nothing else: finish C. Back at A, next neighbour D: its neighbour E is visited, so finish D. A is done: finish A.

Step 2. Outer loop reaches B (unvisited): its neighbour D is visited, so finish B. C, D, E already visited. F is unvisited: finish F.

Step 3. Finish order E, C, D, A, B, F. The finish stack popped from the top gives F, B, A, D, C, E.

Step 4. Check each edge points forward: A→C ✓, A→D ✓, B→D ✓, C→E ✓, D→E ✓. The proposed order A, B, C, D, E, F is also valid; A, C, D, B, E, F is not (edge B→D requires B before D). Add E→A and A → C → E → A is a cycle: DFS would meet A while A is still unfinished, so no order exists.

IN-CLASS · Q5

Hops against total weight

Edges S→A 2, S→B 6, S→T 9, A→B 1, A→T 8, B→T 2. Compare the four S-to-T routes by edge count and total weight.
Show answer
S→T has 1 edge and weight 9. S→A→T has 2 edges and weight 10. S→B→T has 2 edges and weight 8. S→A→B→T has 3 edges and weight 5. The fewest-edge route is S→T but the minimum-weight route is S→A→B→T, result (5, [S, A, B, T]). BFS guarantees the fewest edges, not the lowest weight.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §10.2 Hops are not cost: BFS minimises the number of edges, but the weights add up differently.

Step 1. List all simple S-to-T routes and total each: S→T = 9 (1 edge). S→A→T = 2 + 8 = 10 (2 edges). S→B→T = 6 + 2 = 8 (2 edges). S→A→B→T = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 (3 edges).

Step 2. BFS would return the 1-edge route S→T (cost 9), because it counts edges only. The cheapest route is the 3-edge route S→A→B→T (cost 5).

Step 3. Lesson: for “fewest edges” use BFS; for “lowest total weight” use uniform cost search (next chapter).

IS200, PMSB and DM have no prerequisites; OOAD needs IS200; SE needs OOAD; EI needs OOAD, DM and PMSB; AA needs IS200 and EI; EWS needs SE and EI. Run DFS from IS200 and give one valid study order.

TUTORIAL 9 · TIER 1 · Q4

Make a graph acyclic

Adjacency list A [B, E, F], B [C, D, F], C [D], D [F], E [D, F], F [C]. Which node is visited right after F in DFS from A? Invert one edge to get a DAG and give a topological order.
Show answer

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §9.4 DFS and §9.6 cycles: a cycle is a path that returns to a vertex that is still “in progress”; reversing one edge on the cycle can break it.

Step 1. DFS from A, neighbours alphabetical: A → B → C → D → F; F’s neighbour C is already on the current path (that is the cycle C → D → F → C); F finishes and we back out to A, whose next neighbour is E. So the sequence is A, B, C, D, F, E: E is visited right after F.

Step 2. To remove the cycle C → D → F → C, invert one of its edges. Inverting F→C to C→F gives C [D, F], F [] and no loop remains.

Step 3. A topological order of the resulting DAG: A has no incoming edges so goes first; E needs only A; B needs only A; C after B; D after B, C and E; F after B, C, D, E. One valid order: A, E, B, C, D, F.

Step 2. Stack [A]. Pop A, visit, push B, C → [B, C]. Pop C, visit, push D, F → [B, D, F]. Pop F, visit, push E → [B, D, E]. Pop E, visit (no out-edges). Pop D, visit (its neighbour E is already visited, so nothing to push). Pop B, visit (D and F are visited).

Step 1. Reverse alphabetical push means the alphabetically first neighbour is on top. Stack [A]. Pop A, visit, push B. Pop B, visit, push E, C → C on top. Pop C, visit, push F, D → D on top. Pop D, visit, push G, F → F on top. Pop F, visit, push G.

Step 2. Pop G, visit. The stack still holds E, F, G (with G on top). Pop G: duplicate, discard. Pop F: duplicate, discard. Pop E, visit.

Step 3. Visit sequence A, B, C, D, F, G, E. The weights 2, 3, 1 etc. were never used.

IN-CLASS · Q9

Uniform cost search from A to G

Run UCS on Graph 4 with entries written node(cost, previous). Dequeue the lowest cost, stop when the target is dequeued, update only on a strictly lower cost, and never re-enqueue a dequeued node.
Show answer
Step 1: dequeue A(0), enqueue B(2, A). Step 2: dequeue B(2), enqueue C(5, B) and E(4, B). Step 3: dequeue E(4), enqueue F(9, E). Step 4: dequeue C(5); D(6, C) is enqueued and F via C costs 9, which is not strictly lower, so F is unchanged. Step 5: dequeue D(6); G(7, D) is enqueued and F via D costs 9, unchanged. Step 6: dequeue G(7), the target, and stop. Following previous links gives the path A → B → C → D → G with total cost 7.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §10.3 Uniform cost search: priority queue of node(cost, previous); always dequeue the cheapest; stop when the target is dequeued; update only on a strictly lower cost.

Step 1. Cost of a neighbour = (cost of the node you just dequeued) + (edge weight). Start A(0).

Step 2. Dequeue A(0): B costs 0 + 2 → enqueue B(2, A). Dequeue B(2): C = 2 + 3 = 5 → C(5, B); E = 2 + 2 = 4 → E(4, B). Dequeue E(4) (cheapest): F = 4 + 5 = 9 → F(9, E).

Step 3. Dequeue C(5): D = 5 + 1 = 6 → D(6, C). F via C = 5 + 4 = 9, same as existing 9, not strictly lower, so keep F(9, E). Dequeue D(6): G = 6 + 1 = 7 → G(7, D); F via D = 6 + 3 = 9, again not lower.

Step 4. Now the queue holds F(9) and G(7). Dequeue G(7): it is the target, so stop. Follow previous links backwards: G ← D ← C ← B ← A. Path A → B → C → D → G, cost 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 7.

Check / common slip. We stop when G is dequeued, not when it is first enqueued. At the moment G was enqueued, F(9) was still waiting: only dequeuing G(7) proves nothing cheaper remains.

Show answer
Symmetric, six places: (6−1)!/2 = 60. Direction-dependent: (6−1)! = 120. At 10⁹ tours/s: n = 10 has 181,440 tours (about 0.0002 s); n = 15 has 43,589,145,600 (about 44 s); n = 20 has about 6.1 × 10¹⁶ (about 1.9 years). Going from n to n + 1 multiplies the count by n.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Step 1. Line up 6 places: 6! = 720 orders. A tour is a loop, so rotating the starting place gives the same loop: divide by 6 → 5! = 120. This is the number of tours when the cost depends on direction.

Step 2. If distances are symmetric, running a tour backwards costs the same, so each loop is counted twice: 120 ÷ 2 = 60.

Step 3. General: (n−1)!/2 symmetric and (n−1)! directed. Going from n to n+1 multiplies the count by n.

Step 4. Times at 10⁹ tours per second. n = 10: 9!/2 = 181,440 tours ≈ 0.0002 s. n = 15: 14!/2 = 43,589,145,600 ≈ 44 s. n = 20: 19!/2 ≈ 6.1 × 10¹⁶ tours ≈ 6.1 × 10⁷ s ≈ 1.9 years.
