IN-CLASS · Q2

Nearest neighbour from J and from S

Distances (km): C–J 28, C–N 25, C–P 13, C–S 17, C–W 24, J–N 6, J–P 19, J–S 11, J–W 13, N–P 17, N–S 10, N–W 16, P–S 12, P–W 12, S–W 17. Run nearest neighbour from J and from S.
Show answer
From J: J → N (6) → S (10) → P (12) → W (12) → C (24) → J (28), total 92 km. From S: S → N (10) → J (6) → W (13) → P (12) → C (13) → S (17), total 71 km. The start matters: nearest neighbour is not optimal and the closing leg is never considered. The optimal tour for this data is also 71 km.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.4 Nearest neighbour: from the current city, go to the nearest unvisited city; do not forget the closing leg.

Step 1. From J. Unvisited from J: C 28, N 6, P 19, S 11, W 13 → N (6). From N: C 25, P 17, S 10, W 16 → S (10). From S: C 17, P 12, W 17 → P (12). From P: C 13, W 12 → W (12). From W: only C left (24). Return C → J (28). Total 6 + 10 + 12 + 12 + 24 + 28 = 92 km.

Step 2. From S. From S: C 17, J 11, N 10, P 12, W 17 → N (10). From N: C 25, J 6, P 17, W 16 → J (6). From J: C 28, P 19, W 13 → W (13). From W: C 24, P 12 → P (12). From P: only C (13). Return C → S (17). Total 10 + 6 + 13 + 12 + 13 + 17 = 71 km.

Step 3. Why do the starts differ? The J tour is forced to end with the 24 km hop to C and the 28 km return; the S tour reached C from P (13). Greedy never looks ahead to the closing leg.

Check / common slip. Ties: if two places are equally close, say how you broke the tie (for example alphabetical).

IN-CLASS · Q3

Cheapest-side insertion

Build a tour of the same six places by cheapest-side insertion and compare with nearest neighbour.
Show answer
Start with the closest pair, J and N (6 km). Repeatedly take the outside place closest to a place on the tour and insert it on whichever side of that place adds less. Check both sides, and state how you broke ties because several insertions cost the same. Then compare the final length with 92 km (from J) and 71 km (from S). Following these steps with J–N as the starting pair gives the tour J, S, C, P, W, N (and back to J) of 75 km.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.5 Cheapest-side insertion: start from the closest pair; repeatedly take the outside place x closest to some place y on the tour, and insert it on the side of y that adds less (Δ = d(neighbour, x) + d(x, y) − d(neighbour, y)).

Step 1. Closest pair in the whole table: J–N = 6. Tour: J, N.

Step 2. Outside places and their distance to the nearest tour place: S 10 (to N), W 13 (to J), P 17 (to N), C 25 (to N). Closest is S, anchored at N. Both sides of N are the same edge J–N in a 2-place tour: Δ = 11 + 10 − 6 = 15. Tour J, S, N (27 km).

Step 3. Now P is closest to S (12). Before S (between J and S): 19 + 12 − 11 = 20. After S (between S and N): 12 + 17 − 10 = 19. Take the smaller: insert after S: J, S, P, N (46 km).

Step 4. Next W is closest to P (12). Before P (between S and P): 17 + 12 − 12 = 17. After P (between P and N): 12 + 16 − 17 = 11. Insert after P: J, S, P, W, N (57 km).

Step 5. Last C is closest to P (13). Before P (between S and P): 17 + 13 − 12 = 18. After P (between P and W): 13 + 24 − 12 = 25. Insert before P: J, S, C, P, W, N and back to J. Length 11 + 17 + 13 + 12 + 16 + 6 = 75 km.

Step 6. Compare: nearest neighbour from J gave 92 km, from S gave 71 km, cheapest-side insertion 75 km. The two greedy methods need not agree, and neither is guaranteed optimal.

Check / common slip. Check both sides every time, and state how ties are broken. Different tie rules give different but equally valid tours.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Improve a tour with 2-opt

Starting from the tour J, N, S, P, W, C (92 km), apply 2-opt with best improvement until no move helps. How many 2-opt neighbours does a six-place tour have?
Show answer
A six-place tour has 6(6−3)/2 = 9 neighbours. Best-improvement steps: 92 km, then J, N, S, P, C, W at 78 km, then J, N, S, C, P, W at 71 km, after which no 2-opt move improves. A local optimum need not be a global optimum in general; here 71 km happens to match the best tour.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.6 2-opt: delete two tour edges and reconnect the pieces differently (reverse the stretch between them); keep the move if the tour gets shorter; stop at a local optimum.

Step 1. Neighbours: the first edge can be any of n = 6; the second cannot be the same edge or share a city with it (n − 3 = 3 choices); each pair is counted twice: 6 × 3 / 2 = 9 neighbouring tours.

Step 2. Start J, N, S, P, W, C (92 km). For a move removing edges a–b and c–e and adding a–c and b–e, Δ = d(a,c) + d(b,e) − d(a,b) − d(c,e); negative Δ means shorter.

Step 3. Best of the 9 moves: remove P–W (12) and C–J (28), add P–C (13) and W–J (13): Δ = 26 − 40 = −14. Reverse the stretch W, C: tour J, N, S, P, C, W, 78 km.

Step 4. Next round best move: remove S–P (12) and C–W (24), add S–C (17) and P–W (12): Δ = 29 − 36 = −7. Tour J, N, S, C, P, W, 71 km.

Step 5. Third round: all 9 moves have Δ ≥ 0, so no improvement: a local optimum. Here it also happens to be the best of all 60 tours, but a local optimum is not guaranteed to be the global optimum.

IN-CLASS · Q5

When greedy coin change fails

Coins 1, 5, 6, 9, unlimited. For amounts 11, 12 and 15 give the greedy and an optimal combination.
Show answer
11: greedy 9 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), optimal 5 + 6 (2). 12: greedy 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 (4), optimal 6 + 6 (2). 15: greedy 9 + 6 (2), which is optimal. So largest-coin-first fails for this coin system.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.7 Greedy beyond TSP: greedy takes the largest coin that fits and never reconsiders; it is only right when a proof says so.

Step 1. Greedy for 11: 9, remainder 2, then 1 + 1: three coins (9, 1, 1). Optimal: 5 + 6 = 11 with two coins.

Step 2. Greedy for 12: 9, remainder 3, then 1 + 1 + 1: four coins. Optimal: 6 + 6 = 2 coins. Greedy fails.

Step 3. Greedy for 15: 9, remainder 6, then 6: two coins (9, 6). Optimal as well (no single coin is 15).

Step 4. The counter-examples (11 and 12) show that greedy is not always optimal for the coin system 1, 5, 6, 9: taking the biggest coin first can block a better combination.

IN-CLASS · Q6

Compare the strategies

Compare exhaustive TSP, random TSP search (k tours), nearest neighbour, 2-opt local search and greedy coin change for coins 1, 5, 10, 50.
Show answer
Exhaustive: O(n!) work, works for any input, guaranteed optimal. Random search: O(kn), any input, no guarantee. Nearest neighbour: O(n²), any input, no guarantee. 2-opt: O(n²) per iteration, any starting tour, ends at a local optimum with no guarantee of the global optimum. Greedy coin change for 1, 5, 10, 50: very cheap, and optimal for that particular coin system.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.3 baselines and §11.4–11.6 heuristics: compare what each guarantees and what it costs.

Step 1. Exhaustive (try all (n−1)!/2 tours): cost O(n!), works for any input, and is guaranteed optimal.

Step 2. Random search (sample k tours): O(kn), works for any input, no guarantee.

Step 3. Nearest neighbour: n − 1 steps each scanning up to n cities, O(n²), any input, no guarantee.

Step 4. 2-opt: O(n²) neighbours per iteration, needs a starting tour, ends at a local optimum with no guarantee of the global optimum.

Step 5. Greedy coin change for 1, 5, 10, 50: a few subtractions, essentially instant. For this particular coin system each coin divides the next, so greedy is provably optimal.

Check / common slip. The pattern is the “pick two” trade-off of §11.2: speed, quality, generality. Greedy gives speed and generality but only sometimes quality.

TUTORIAL 11 · TIER 1 · Q2

Two greedy tours on seven cities

From the distance table on the sheet, give the tour from the first greedy algorithm starting at A, and from the second greedy algorithm starting with the closest pair.
Show answer
Answer key: nearest neighbour A → D → C → G → E → F → B → A with cost 861 (its mirror is also fine). Cheapest-side insertion C → D → A → G → E → F → B → C with cost 816 (mirrors and rotations are also fine).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.4 Nearest neighbour and §11.5 cheapest-side insertion on seven cities (the distance table is on the tutorial sheet).

Step 1. First greedy algorithm (nearest neighbour from A): repeatedly look at the row of the current city, pick the smallest entry among unvisited cities, move there, and at the end add the leg back to A. The answer key’s tour is A → D → C → G → E → F → B → A, cost 861; its mirror image is equally correct.

Step 2. Second greedy algorithm (cheapest-side insertion): start with the closest pair of all (the smallest number in the table), then repeatedly choose the outside city closest to some tour city and insert it on the cheaper side of that city. The key’s tour is C → D → A → G → E → F → B → C, cost 816. Rotations and mirrors are the same tour.

Step 3. To mark yourself: add the leg lengths of the tour including the return to the start; both answers should match the keys within tie-break differences.

TUTORIAL 11 · TIER 1 · Q3

Greedy path in a tree

The greedy rule moves to the child with the higher value from the root to a leaf. Apply it to the tutorial tree, then give a tree where it fails.
Show answer
On the tutorial tree greedy gives 8 + 21 + 9 + 12 = 50. A failure example from the key: greedy takes the path with sum 1 + 3 = 4 while the optimal path is 1 + 2 + 5 = 8, because a smaller child can lead to a much larger descendant.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.7 Greedy beyond TSP: a greedy rule makes the locally best choice at every step; it fails when that choice blocks a larger payoff later.

Step 1. Greedy on the tutorial tree: from the root take the child with the higher value, then the same again to a leaf: 8 + 21 + 9 + 12 = 50.

Step 2. A failing tree (the key’s example): root 1 with children 2 and 3, where 3 is a leaf and 2 has a child worth 5. Greedy picks 3 (the bigger child) and ends with 1 + 3 = 4, while 1 + 2 + 5 = 8 is better. A smaller child can lead to a much larger descendant.

TUTORIAL 11 · TIER 1 · Q4

Coins 20, 10, 5, 1

Design a brute-force and a greedy algorithm for change. Does greedy ever fail for these coins?
Show answer
Brute force: try all subsets of size 1, then size 2, and so on, until one pays the amount. Greedy: repeatedly deduct the largest denomination that fits. For 20, 10, 5, 1 greedy never fails (answer: no).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.7 Greedy coin change works when each coin value divides the next larger one.

Step 1. Brute force: try every combination: first all single coins, then all pairs, then triples, … until some combination pays the amount exactly; the first success uses the fewest coins.

Step 2. Greedy: repeatedly subtract the largest coin that is not more than what is left. Example 47 with 20, 10, 5, 1: 20, 20, then 5, 1, 1: five coins.

Step 3. For 20, 10, 5, 1, greedy never fails: each coin divides the next larger one (1 | 5 | 10 | 20), so replacing smaller coins by the bigger one never costs extra coins. No failure. (Contrast 1, 5, 6, 9, where 6 does not divide 9 and greedy fails.)

TUTORIAL 11 · TIER 1 · Q5

Knapsack with a 15 kg bag

Items A (12 kg, $10), B (5 kg, $8), C (4 kg, $2), D (3 kg, $5), E (2 kg, $6). Describe brute force and greedy, and say whether greedy can fail for some limit.
Show answer
Brute force: try all subsets (5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 combinations by size). Greedy: repeatedly add the item with the best value-to-weight ratio until the limit would be breached; a smallest-weight-first rule is another option. Greedy can fail, for example with a 7 kg limit (E then D gives $11, but B + E gives $14).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §11.7 Greedy beyond TSP: knapsack with a weight limit; the greedy rule must be named and may still fail.

Step 1. Brute force: there are 2⁵ = 32 subsets (1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 by size); discard those over 15 kg and keep the best value.

Step 2. Greedy by value-to-weight: A 10/12 ≈ 0.83, B 8/5 = 1.6, C 2/4 = 0.5, D 5/3 ≈ 1.67, E 6/2 = 3. Take E (2 kg, $6), D (3 kg, $5), B (5 kg, $8): 10 kg, $19. A (12 kg) no longer fits; C (4 kg) fits: 14 kg, $21.

Step 3. It can fail: with a 7 kg limit greedy takes E (2 kg) then D (3 kg) = 5 kg, $11; then nothing else fits (B needs 5). But B + E = 7 kg gives $14. So greedy is not always optimal.
